---
title: NetworkX backend
guide-section: "Interoperability"
---

[NetworkX](https://networkx.org) can hand its function calls to other libraries, called
*backends*. EdgeCase is one: when it is installed alongside NetworkX, code written for NetworkX can
run on EdgeCase's Rust core, unchanged except for how the call is dispatched. This is a different
route from the conversions in [Other libraries](other-libraries.qmd): the graph stays a NetworkX
graph in your code, and NetworkX converts it to EdgeCase behind the scenes.

## Dispatching a call

Name the backend in a single call:

```{python}
import networkx as nx

G = nx.karate_club_graph()
bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(G, backend="edgecase")
max(bc, key=bc.get)
```

Or prefer EdgeCase for every call it implements, for a whole session:

```{python}
nx.config.backend_priority.algos = ["edgecase"]
communities = nx.community.louvain_communities(G, seed=42)
[sorted(c) for c in communities]
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
nx.config.backend_priority.algos = []
```

Setting the environment variable `NETWORKX_BACKEND_PRIORITY=edgecase` before starting Python does
the same. Functions that EdgeCase does not implement run in NetworkX as usual.

## Conversion and caching

NetworkX converts a graph to EdgeCase the first time a function needs it, and caches the result
on the graph (in `G.__networkx_cache__`), so later calls on the same, unchanged graph reuse it.
Only the attributes a function needs are converted, such as the `weight` of a weighted algorithm.

The conversion costs about as much as one pass over the graph. For functions that cost little
more than that themselves (connected components, traversals, most single-source searches,
matrix exports), automatic dispatch uses EdgeCase only when a converted graph is already cached;
naming the backend with `backend="edgecase"` always uses it.

A converted graph can also be kept explicitly. NetworkX functions given it run on EdgeCase
without converting again:

```{python}
from edgecase.nx_backend import from_networkx

EG = from_networkx(
    G, preserve_edge_attrs=True, preserve_node_attrs=True, preserve_graph_attrs=True
)
round(nx.pagerank(EG)[0], 6) == round(nx.pagerank(G)[0], 6)
```

To pass such a graph to a function EdgeCase does not implement, set
`nx.config.fallback_to_nx = True`, so NetworkX converts it back.

## What is covered

EdgeCase implements over 200 NetworkX functions, from components, traversals and shortest paths to
centralities, community detection, flows, matchings, graph hashes, relabeling and matrix exports.
The current list:

```{python}
functions = sorted(nx.utils.backends.backend_info["edgecase"]["functions"])
len(functions), functions[:10]
```

Each of these functions' NetworkX docstrings also gains a *Backends* section naming EdgeCase.

## The same answers as NetworkX

The backend aims to return exactly what NetworkX returns: the same values (floating-point sums
included, by adding in NetworkX's order), the same order of dictionaries, lists and generators,
and the same errors. Randomized algorithms such as Louvain and asynchronous label propagation draw
the same random numbers from `seed` as NetworkX and return the same partitions.

A few functions can return a different but equally valid answer, or one that differs in an
unimportant way:

| Function | Difference |
| :-- | :-- |
| `leiden_communities`, `leiden_partitions` | a different valid partition for the same `seed` (NetworkX's depends on the iteration order of Python sets) |
| `max_weight_matching`, `min_weight_matching` | possibly another matching of the same weight and size |
| `maximum_flow` | possibly another maximum flow; the flow value and `minimum_cut` are the same |
| `adamic_adar_index`, `resource_allocation_index`, `ra_index_soundarajan_hopcroft` | possibly a difference in the last bit for pairs with three or more common neighbors (NetworkX adds over a Python set, whose order for string nodes changes with `PYTHONHASHSEED`) |
| `generalized_degree` | equal `Counter`s, whose keys can be in another order |
| shortest-path lengths (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford) | on graphs that mix integer and float weights, float distances where NetworkX keeps integers on all-integer paths (the values are equal) |
| `find_cliques`, `greedy_color` (set-ordered strategies), `maximal_independent_set`, `dominating_set` | these reproduce NetworkX's order by modelling CPython's set iteration, so on other interpreters or untested versions (outside CPython 3.10-3.14) NetworkX runs them instead |

## Running NetworkX's test suite on EdgeCase

NetworkX's own tests can be run with EdgeCase as the backend: each NetworkX call that EdgeCase
implements is converted, run on EdgeCase, and checked by the tests. From a clone of EdgeCase, with
NetworkX's test dependencies installed:

```bash
scripts/run_nx_tests.sh -n 8
```

The suite passes; the few tests marked as expected failures, each with its reason, are listed in
`python/edgecase/nx_backend/_testing.py`.
